narrative:
The model predicted a 58% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

Your rejection was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. The strongest influence came from your third-year class ranking. Placing in the first decile of your class—far below the average of roughly the sixth decile among accepted students—strongly pushed the prediction toward failure. This single piece of information had the largest impact on the outcome.

Next, your undergraduate GPA of 2.90, which sits noticeably below the 3.23 average of accepted students, worked in the opposite direction. It provided some positive signal that you could still pass the bar, partially offsetting the negative outlook, but not enough to change the final result.

The third most important factor was your plan to attend law school part-time. Only 7% of accepted students choose part-time study, and this choice added further weight toward predicting failure.

Taken together, your lower class standing, combined with part-time enrollment plans, outweighed the encouraging effect of your undergraduate record and led the model to conclude you were more likely than not to fail the bar exam.

What you should do next is straightforward: retake key courses to raise your class rank, consider full-time study if possible, and then reapply. Improving those two controllable factors would likely shift future predictions in your favor. (248 words)
